objects.notes: AI policy framework maps directly to Art. 17 QMS requirements — policies, governance documentation, and management commitment are core QMS artefacts.
AI policy documents form part of the technical file required for conformity assessment under Art. 43.
Policy framework establishes the organisational commitment to risk management, which is the foundation of the Art. 9 risk management system.
Organisational roles and responsibilities are a mandatory component of the QMS under Art. 17(1)(a).
Designated AI Owner role aligns with the responsible person required to conduct the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment under Art. 27.
Adequate computational resources and tooling directly support the accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity requirements of Art. 15.
Resource governance includes controls over input data pipelines, supporting Art. 26(5) deployer obligations on input data management.
AI system impact assessment is structurally equivalent to the Art. 9 risk management system — both require lifecycle risk identification, estimation, and evaluation.
Impact assessment includes risk identification and analysis per A.5.2-3, directly mapping to Art. 9(2) risk identification requirements.
Risk estimation and severity evaluation in impact assessment maps to Art. 9(4) risk estimation and evaluation requirements.
High-risk AI FRIA requirement (Art. 27) is a specialisation of the general impact assessment obligation in A.5.
Development governance controls (design specs, approval gates) are core elements of the QMS under Art. 17.
Development governance generates the technical documentation required under Art. 11 — design specifications, testing results, and model documentation.
Development governance includes data governance requirements for training datasets, aligning with Art. 10 data governance obligations.
Post-deployment monitoring in the AI lifecycle directly implements Art. 72 post-market monitoring obligations.
Incident response in the AI lifecycle maps to serious incident reporting obligations under Art. 73.
Operational monitoring and logging requirements in A.6.2 implement Art. 12 automatic logging obligations.
A.7 data governance requirements map directly to Art. 10 data governance obligations for training, validation, and test datasets.
Data quality assurance requirements in A.7.3 map directly to Art. 10(3) data quality criteria.
Bias detection and mitigation in A.7.4 maps to Art. 10(5) bias examination and monitoring requirements.
Special categories of data handling in A.7.5 maps to Art. 10(6) special data categories provisions.
Technical documentation obligations in A.8 support Art. 11 technical documentation requirements for regulators.
User-facing disclosures in A.8.3-4 map to Art. 13 transparency obligations to deployers and users.
Notifications to affected persons in A.8.5 align with Art. 50 information obligations to affected individuals.
Human oversight design requirements in A.9.2 map directly to Art. 14 human oversight design obligations.
Override capability requirements in A.9.3 map to Art. 14(4)(d) stop/pause capability obligations.
AI output interpretation safeguards in A.9.3 align with Art. 14(4)(a) output interpretation requirements.
Deployer oversight obligations in A.9.4 align with Art. 26 deployer responsibilities including oversight measures.
Third-party AI provider management includes obligations around Art. 49 EU AI database registration that cascades through the supply chain.
Customer relationship controls include input data management obligations passed to deployers under Art. 26(5).
Third-party risk management in A.10 contributes to risk mitigation measures required under Art. 9(6).
AI policy framework is the primary implementation mechanism for GOVERN 1 — policies, processes, and accountability structures for AI risk management.
AI governance policies address accountability and transparency requirements covered under GOVERN 2.
Organisational roles and responsibilities are a direct implementation of GOVERN 1 accountability structures.
Role assignments and reporting structures implement GOVERN 2 transparency and accountability requirements.
Internal AI governance structures support GOVERN 3 team diversity, bias awareness, and stakeholder engagement.
Resource governance provides the operational context and constraints needed for MAP 1 AI context classification.
Tooling and competence resources underpin the scientific and technical knowledge requirements in MAP 2.
Impact assessment provides the risk context classification required by MAP 1 — understanding the deployment context and potential harms.
Impact assessment methodology maps to MAP 2 scientific grounding for risk assessment.
AI-specific harm assessment in A.5 maps to MAP 3 AI risk identification and prioritisation.
Likelihood and severity evaluation in impact assessment supports MAP 5 risk measurement and prioritisation.
Development governance policies and processes are a primary implementation of GOVERN 1 risk management practices.
Design governance including intended use specification implements MAP 1 context and use case classification.
Development approval gates and governance controls implement MANAGE 1 risk treatment and response decisions.
Lifecycle management including change control and incident response implements MANAGE 1 risk response actions.
Operational monitoring and drift detection in A.6.2 implements MANAGE 2 risk monitoring and correction.
Feedback loops and continuous improvement in lifecycle management support MANAGE 3 corrective actions and risk mitigation.
Operational performance monitoring implements MEASURE 3 AI system performance tracking and evaluation.
Data provenance and quality documentation supports MAP 2 scientific and technical knowledge about AI risks.
Data quality measurement and thresholds implement MEASURE 1 AI risk identification and measurement methods.
Bias detection and mitigation metrics in A.7.4 implement MEASURE 2 AI trustworthiness evaluation.
Data quality monitoring and correction processes implement MANAGE 2 ongoing risk monitoring for data-related issues.
Stakeholder information practices implement GOVERN 4 organisational teams and accountability for AI transparency.
Transparency and disclosure practices align with GOVERN 5 policies for AI transparency and explainability.
Stakeholder engagement and communication processes support GOVERN 6 policies for managing AI risks across the organisation.
Oversight mechanisms and performance safeguards implement MEASURE 3 AI system performance and effectiveness evaluation.
Misuse safeguards and contestability mechanisms implement MEASURE 4 feedback and improvement processes.
Human oversight and override capabilities implement MANAGE 3 risk response and corrective actions for AI misuse or failure.
Responsible use controls and safeguards implement MANAGE 4 residual risk monitoring and continuous improvement.
Third-party AI risk management implements GOVERN 3 — organisational roles for managing AI risks from suppliers and partners.
Third-party AI due diligence and supplier risk classification implement MAP 4 risk prioritisation for acquired AI components.
Ongoing third-party monitoring and contractual controls implement MANAGE 4 residual risk management in the AI supply chain.
AI policy framework is the organisational accountability mechanism — policies, commitments, and governance structures directly implement OECD Principle 5 accountability obligations for AI actors.
AI policy establishes transparency commitments — objectives, scope, and stakeholder expectations align with OECD Principle 3 transparency and responsible disclosure.
Organisational roles, responsibilities, and oversight structures directly implement OECD Principle 5 accountability requirements — defining who is accountable for AI systems and their outcomes.
Adequate human, technical, and computational resources are foundational to building and maintaining robust, secure and safe AI systems as required by OECD Principle 4.

AI system impact assessment evaluates societal, environmental, and individual harms and benefits — the primary instrument for implementing OECD Principle 1 inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being.
Impact assessment addresses human rights, dignity, non-discrimination, privacy, and fairness considerations — directly implementing OECD Principle 2 human-centred values and fairness.
Responsible AI development governance — design specifications, testing, verification, and approval gates — implements OECD Principle 4 lifecycle robustness, security and safety.

Operational monitoring, drift detection, and incident response ensure continued safety and reliability — OECD Principle 4 requires AI systems to remain robust and secure throughout their entire lifecycle.
Bias detection, mitigation, and fair data practices in A.7 directly implement OECD Principle 2 — AI systems should not produce unfair or discriminatory outcomes.
Data quality, provenance, and integrity controls in A.7 are foundational to the reliability and robustness required by OECD Principle 4.
A.8 transparency and disclosure requirements are the direct implementation of OECD Principle 3 — technical documentation, user information, and responsible disclosure across the AI system lifecycle.
Human oversight, override capabilities, and contestability mechanisms preserve human agency and dignity — OECD Principle 2 requires AI to respect human autonomy and democratic values.
Responsible use controls and accountability for AI decisions and outputs implement OECD Principle 5 — organisations must be accountable for the proper functioning of their AI systems.
Third-party AI supply chain accountability — provider, supplier, and customer risk management — extends OECD Principle 5 accountability obligations across the AI value chain.
ISO 42001 A.5 impact assessment requirement is the primary organisational obligation that ISO/IEC 42005:2025 operationalises — Clause 5.7-5.8 defines how to perform the assessment that A.5 mandates.
ISO 42001 A.5 impact documentation requirements align with ISO 42005 Clause 6.8 — actual and reasonably foreseeable impacts must be identified, documented, and addressed.
ISO 42001 development governance generates AI system information required in ISO 42005 Clause 6.2-6.3 — system description, functionalities, purposes, and intended/unintended uses.
ISO 42001 A.7 data governance maps directly to ISO 42005 Clause 6.4 data information and quality documentation — data sources, quality criteria, and data management practices.
ISO 42001 A.8 transparency documentation includes deployment context and stakeholder communication — aligned with ISO 42005 Clause 6.6-6.7 deployment environment and interested parties documentation.

AI policy framework is an extension of the information security policy set — A.2.2-4 AI governance policies must be integrated with the organisation's overall ISO 27001 information security policy hierarchy.
AI governance roles (AI Owner, AI Risk function) extend the information security roles structure established under A.5.2 — both are accountability frameworks for responsible technology governance.
AI roles and responsibilities (A.3.2-3) are a direct specialisation of information security roles — the AI Owner and AI governance structure sits within and extends the A.5.2 ISMS role framework.

Top management AI governance obligations in A.3.2-3 directly extend A.5.4 management responsibilities — AI risk accountability is a component of overall management responsibility for information security.

AI systems, models, datasets, and tooling environments are information assets under A.5.9 — the AI system resources inventory in A.4.2-6 is a specialisation of the broader asset inventory requirement.

AI compute infrastructure frequently runs on cloud platforms — A.4.2-6 resource governance for cloud-hosted AI systems must integrate with the A.5.23 information security controls for cloud service use.

AI system impact assessment draws on threat intelligence — A.5.7 threat intelligence about adversarial ML attacks, data poisoning, model theft, and AI-specific vulnerabilities informs the A.5 impact assessment process.

AI model vulnerabilities (adversarial robustness failures, training data exposures) are in scope for A.8.8 technical vulnerability management — impact assessment identifies AI-specific vulnerability exposure.

AI model code, training scripts, and pipeline configurations are source code assets under A.8.4 — A.6.1 AI development governance must incorporate access controls and integrity protections consistent with A.8.4.
AI model parameters, hyperparameter configurations, and pipeline settings are configuration items — A.6.1 development governance requires configuration management practices consistent with A.8.9.

AI system development must incorporate secure coding practices — A.6.1 development governance extends A.8.28 secure coding requirements to include AI-specific security considerations (input validation, output sanitisation, model hardening).

AI operational incidents (model failures, adversarial events, unexpected outputs) are information security incidents under A.5.24 — A.6.2 lifecycle incident response requirements are a specialisation of the broader incident management planning obligation.

AI operational monitoring for drift, performance degradation, and anomalous behaviour is a specialisation of A.8.16 monitoring activities — A.6.2 monitoring requirements extend and complement the general information system monitoring framework.

Training data and model inference data containing sensitive information require data masking and pseudonymisation consistent with A.8.11 — A.7.2-6 data governance must incorporate data masking requirements for AI datasets.

AI training datasets, model outputs, and extracted data representations are in scope for A.8.12 data leakage prevention — A.7.2-6 data governance includes controls to prevent unauthorised exfiltration of AI data assets.

AI system disclosures, technical documentation, and information provided to deployers and users are information transfer activities governed by A.5.14 — A.8.2-5 transparency requirements implement A.5.14 in the AI context.

Privileged access to AI model parameters, training pipelines, and inference infrastructure must be managed consistently with A.8.2 — A.9.2-4 human oversight controls include access governance for authorised operators.

AI provider and third-party vendor agreements must include information security requirements consistent with A.5.20 — A.10.2-4 third-party AI governance directly extends the supplier agreement security requirements to AI-specific obligations.

AI supply chain risks (pre-trained model integrity, dataset provenance, component sourcing) are ICT supply chain security issues governed by A.5.21 — A.10.2-4 third-party management must address AI-specific supply chain threats.

AI impact assessment evaluates the conditions under which AI systems collect and process PII — A.5.2-5 assessment obligations directly support ISO 27701 A.1.2 conditions for collection and processing as they apply to AI-driven data flows.

AI impact assessment including FRIA addresses obligations to individuals whose data is processed by AI systems — A.5.2-5 is the primary mechanism for identifying and addressing ISO 27701 A.1.3 PII principal obligations in AI contexts.

AI system impact assessment embeds privacy by design evaluation — A.5.2-5 requires assessing privacy impacts and mitigation measures, which is the operational implementation of ISO 27701 A.1.4 privacy by design and privacy by default for AI systems.

AI data governance (A.7.2-6) directly governs PII collection and processing in training datasets — ISO 27701 A.1.2 conditions for PII processing apply to every AI training data pipeline and must be addressed through the A.7 data governance framework.

Privacy-preserving AI data practices (anonymisation, pseudonymisation, data minimisation in A.7.2-6) implement privacy by design for AI training data — directly aligned with ISO 27701 A.1.4 privacy by design requirements for PII processing.

AI data pipelines involving third-party datasets, data enrichment, or model sharing create PII transfer obligations — A.7.2-6 data governance must address ISO 27701 A.1.5 PII sharing, transfer, and disclosure requirements for AI data flows.

AI transparency disclosures to affected individuals — including explanations of automated decisions — directly implement ISO 27701 A.1.3 obligations to PII principals when AI systems process personal data to generate outputs affecting individuals.

AI system development governance must incorporate privacy into the development lifecycle — A.6.1 development governance extends ISO 27701 A.3.27 secure development life cycle to include privacy-preserving design, differential privacy techniques, and PII minimisation from design stage.

AI system architecture design decisions in A.6.1 must incorporate privacy-preserving architectural principles — ISO 27701 A.3.29 secure system architecture and engineering principles apply to AI system design, including model architecture choices that affect PII exposure.

Third-party AI providers frequently involve PII transfer — A.10.2-4 third-party relationship management must address ISO 27701 A.1.5 PII sharing, transfer, and disclosure obligations when AI providers process personal data on behalf of the organisation.

AI governance policies are a component of the organisation's policy for managing technology risks — A.2.2-4 AI policy framework implements NIST CSF GV.PO-01 by establishing and maintaining AI-specific policies aligned with the risk management strategy.

AI governance commitments and ethical principles reflect the organisational mission context — A.2.2-4 ensures AI policies are informed by and aligned with NIST CSF GV.OC-01 organisational mission and strategic context.

AI governance requires designated leadership accountability for AI-related risks — A.3.2-3 AI Owner and governance structure directly implements NIST CSF GV.RR-01 leadership responsibility and accountability for AI risks.

AI roles, responsibilities, and reporting structures are the AI-domain implementation of NIST CSF GV.RR-02 — A.3.2-3 defines cybersecurity and AI risk roles, authorities, and escalation paths for the AI management system.

Adequate computational, tooling, and human resources for AI systems implement NIST CSF GV.RR-03 — A.4.2-6 ensures adequate resources are allocated commensurate with AI risk management requirements and commitments.

AI systems, models, datasets, and tooling environments are software and services that must be inventoried — A.4.2-6 AI system resources governance implements NIST CSF ID.AM-02 inventories of software, services, and systems for AI assets.

AI system impact assessment evaluates potential impacts and likelihoods of AI-specific threats — A.5.2-5 directly implements NIST CSF ID.RA-04 by identifying and analysing threats exploiting AI system vulnerabilities and their consequences.

Impact assessment requires understanding threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts specific to AI systems — A.5.2-5 provides the structured methodology for implementing NIST CSF ID.RA-05 risk analysis for AI system deployments.

Impact assessment outputs drive risk response selection, prioritisation, and tracking for AI systems — A.5.2-5 assessment results directly inform NIST CSF ID.RA-06 risk response planning and monitoring for identified AI risks.

AI system development must integrate secure software development practices — A.6.1 development governance implements NIST CSF PR.PS-06 by requiring security reviews, testing, approval gates, and responsible AI principles throughout the AI development lifecycle.

AI model configurations, pipeline parameters, and deployment specifications are configuration items — A.6.1 development governance implements NIST CSF PR.PS-01 configuration management practices for AI system components.

AI operational monitoring for model drift, performance degradation, and anomalous behaviour implements NIST CSF DE.CM-09 — A.6.2 lifecycle monitoring continuously assesses AI computing environments for potential problems.

AI incident response as part of lifecycle management implements NIST CSF RS.MA-01 — A.6.2 incident response for AI system failures, adversarial events, and unexpected outputs is executed per the organisation's incident response plan.

AI training datasets and stored model artefacts require confidentiality, integrity, and availability protections — A.7.2-6 data governance implements NIST CSF PR.DS-01 data at rest protections for AI data assets.

AI training datasets, validation sets, and data pipeline metadata must be inventoried — A.7.2-6 data governance implements NIST CSF ID.AM-07 inventories of data and corresponding metadata for AI data assets used in model training and inference.

AI transparency and disclosure to stakeholders implements NIST CSF GV.OC-02 — A.8.2-5 provides information about AI systems to internal stakeholders, deployers, users, and affected persons, establishing the stakeholder communication required by GV.OC-02.

Access permissions for AI system operators, reviewers, and override authorities implement NIST CSF PR.AA-05 — A.9.2-4 human oversight controls require defined access authorisations to AI systems, consistent with the principle of least privilege.

Third-party AI provider risk management implements NIST CSF GV.SC-01 — A.10.2-4 establishes the AI supply chain risk management programme, including policies, processes, and accountabilities for managing AI provider and supplier risks.

Due diligence on AI providers and suppliers before engagement implements NIST CSF GV.SC-06 — A.10.2-4 third-party AI due diligence reduces supply chain risk through pre-acquisition assessment of AI component integrity and vendor trustworthiness.

AI policy framework (A.2.2-4) maps to ISO27018 A.2 consent and choice — AI systems that collect and process PII must implement the consent mechanisms required by A.2; the AI policy must address the lawful basis for all AI training data and inference data collection.

AI governance roles (A.3.2-3) map to ISO27018 A.10 accountability — AI owners and the AI risk function are accountable for PII processed by AI systems; the accountability chain from A.3.2-3 role assignments must extend to all PII processing by AI.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to ISO27018 A.1 general principles — AI risk assessments must identify all PII processing activities and associated risks; the general ISO 27018 principles apply to AI-system PII processing as a foundational constraint.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to ISO27018 A.3 purpose legitimacy — AI risk assessments must evaluate whether training data collection and inference use are aligned with documented legitimate purposes; purpose deviation is an AI-specific PII risk.

AI governance objectives (A.5.2-5) map to ISO27018 A.5 data minimisation — AI systems must collect and retain the minimum PII necessary for the AI task; data minimisation is both an AI governance objective and a core ISO 27018 requirement for PII in public cloud.

AI governance objectives (A.5.2-5) map to ISO27018 A.7 accuracy and quality — AI governance requires data quality objectives; the accuracy of PII used in AI training directly affects model output quality and must meet ISO 27018 accuracy requirements.

AI operational planning (A.6.1) maps to ISO27018 A.6 use, retention and disclosure limitation — AI system operational plans must define retention periods and use restrictions for all PII; A.6.1 resource planning must address PII data lifecycle management.

AI operations (A.7.2-6) map to ISO27018 A.2 consent and choice — operational AI systems collecting PII must ensure valid consent or other lawful basis is maintained throughout the AI lifecycle; re-use of training data for new purposes requires fresh consent under A.2.

AI operations (A.7.2-6) map to ISO27018 A.4 collection limitation — AI data collection pipelines must implement technical controls limiting PII collection to specified purposes; automated data ingestion for AI training must not exceed the collection limitations in A.4.

AI performance and security (A.8.2-5) map to ISO27018 A.11 information security — AI systems processing PII must implement the information security controls specified in A.11; AI security measures (model access controls, inference API security) are a component of A.11 compliance.

AI impact assessment (A.9.2-4) maps to ISO27018 A.8 openness, transparency and notice — AI impact assessments must evaluate the transparency of AI decision-making that uses PII; data subjects must be informed when PII is used in AI systems as required by A.8.

AI improvement processes (A.10.2-4) map to ISO27018 A.12 privacy compliance — AI system improvement cycles must include privacy compliance reviews; changes to AI models or training data that affect PII processing require privacy impact assessment under A.12.

AI policy framework (A.2.2-4) maps to EU CRA MAN.1 — AI systems classified as products with digital elements under the CRA require a product cybersecurity policy; A.2.2-4 AI governance policies must integrate CRA essential requirements for AI products.

AI governance roles (A.3.2-3) map to EU CRA MAN.2 — AI owners responsible for AI system security must also fulfil CRA accountability roles; A.3.2-3 role structures must include CRA-designated product security responsibility.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to EU CRA VUL.1 — AI-specific vulnerabilities (adversarial attacks, model poisoning, training data manipulation) must be identified and tracked; A.4.2-6 risk assessment methodology must encompass CRA vulnerability management requirements.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to EU CRA MAN.4 — regulatory compliance risk for AI systems includes CRA obligations; A.4.2-6 risk assessments must address CRA conformity requirements for AI products and high-risk AI systems.

AI governance objectives (A.5.2-5) map to EU CRA SEC.6 — AI security by design is required; AI governance objectives must include CRA security-by-design essential requirements; AI system security objectives should directly reference CRA essential requirements applicable to the AI product category.

AI operational planning (A.6.1) maps to EU CRA MAN.3 — AI supply chain security is required; operational planning for AI systems must address the security of AI frameworks, pre-trained models, and third-party AI components; CRA SBOM requirements apply to AI software components.

AI operations (A.7.2-6) map to EU CRA SEC.6 — AI system operations must maintain security-by-design controls throughout the operational lifecycle; operational changes to AI systems must be assessed against CRA essential requirements.

AI data management (A.7.2-6) maps to EU CRA SEC.4 — attack surface minimisation for AI systems includes restricting access to training pipelines, model artefacts, and inference APIs; A.7.2-6 operational data management must address AI-specific attack surface reduction.

AI performance and security (A.8.2-5) map to EU CRA SEC.7 — AI systems processing personal data must implement data protection by design; A.8.2-5 AI security monitoring must include detection of PII leakage through AI outputs (inference attacks, model extraction).

AI security monitoring (A.8.2-5) maps to EU CRA VUL.2 — AI vulnerability disclosure must include AI-specific vulnerability classes; A.8.2-5 monitoring for AI model degradation and adversarial attacks must feed into the CRA coordinated vulnerability disclosure programme.

AI impact assessment (A.9.2-4) maps to EU CRA VUL.1 — AI impact assessments are a risk-based vulnerability management input; identified AI risks that represent security vulnerabilities must be tracked and remediated under the CRA vulnerability management programme.

AI improvement processes (A.10.2-4) map to EU CRA VUL.4 — AI system improvements driven by identified vulnerabilities must be tracked; A.10.2-4 continual improvement loops for AI security directly implement the CRA vulnerability tracking and remediation cycle.

AI policy framework (A.2.2-4) maps to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(b) incident handling — AI governance policies must address AI-specific incidents (model failure, adversarial attacks, data poisoning); AI incident handling procedures are a component of the NIS2 incident management capability.

AI governance roles (A.3.2-3) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(b) incident handling — AI owners and risk functions must be integrated into the incident response team; AI-specific incident roles contribute to the comprehensive incident handling capability required by NIS2.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(a) risk analysis — AI risk assessments are a component of the risk analysis required by Art. 21(2)(a); AI risks to network and information systems must be included in the organisational risk management framework.

AI governance objectives (A.5.2-5) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(b) security measures — AI security objectives must include NIS2-required security measures; AI system security capabilities (availability, integrity, confidentiality) align with NIS2 security measure requirements.

AI governance objectives (A.5.2-5) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(e) security in acquisition — AI system acquisition and development must follow secure development practices; AI governance objectives for security in the development lifecycle implement Art. 21(2)(e) requirements.

AI operational planning (A.6.1) maps to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(d) supply chain security — AI operational planning must address AI supply chain risks (pre-trained models, AI frameworks, data suppliers); NIS2 supply chain security requirements apply to AI component suppliers.

AI operations (A.7.2-6) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(e) security in acquisition — AI operational procedures must ensure that AI components meet security requirements throughout the system lifecycle; Art. 21(2)(e) security requirements apply to AI system maintenance and updates.

AI performance and security monitoring (A.8.2-5) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(b) security capability — AI security monitoring contributes to the detection capability required for incident handling; AI system availability and integrity monitoring implements NIS2 security measure requirements.

AI security controls (A.8.2-5) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(j) MFA and communications — AI management interfaces must require MFA; AI API access must use secured communications; A.8.2-5 AI security controls must include Art. 21(2)(j) authentication requirements for AI systems.

AI impact assessment (A.9.2-4) maps to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(a) risk analysis — AI impact assessments are a specialised form of risk analysis; their findings must be incorporated into the comprehensive risk analysis required by Art. 21(2)(a) for network and information systems.

AI improvement processes (A.10.2-4) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(a) risk analysis — ongoing AI improvement cycles include reassessment of AI risks; continual improvement of AI security is a component of the dynamic risk analysis required by NIS2.

AI governance roles (A.3.2-3) map to NIS2 Art. 21(2)(g) training — AI owners and risk functions require NIS2-aligned cybersecurity training; AI governance staff must be included in the cybersecurity awareness and training programme required by Art. 21(2)(g).

AI policy framework (A.2.2-4) maps to CSA AICM GRC-01 governance policy — the AI governance policy framework required by A.2.2-4 must integrate with the cloud security governance policy in GRC-01; AI policy is a specialised component of the broader cloud governance policy.

AI policy framework (A.2.2-4) maps to CSA AICM GRC-09 acceptable use of AI — AI governance policies must define acceptable use boundaries for AI services; A.2.2-4 AI policy framework and GRC-09 acceptable use policy are corollary governance requirements.

AI governance roles (A.3.2-3) map to CSA AICM GRC-12 ethics committee — AI governance roles must include an ethics and fairness review function; A.3.2-3 AI governance structures should incorporate or interface with the ethics committee required by GRC-12.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to CSA AICM GRC-10 AI impact assessment — AI risk assessments required by A.4.2-6 and AI impact assessments required by GRC-10 are directly corollary obligations; both mandate systematic evaluation of AI system risks to individuals and society.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to CSA AICM GRC-11 bias and fairness assessment — AI risk assessments must include evaluation of algorithmic bias; A.4.2-6 risk assessment scope must address fairness and non-discrimination risks identified in GRC-11.

AI governance objectives (A.5.2-5) map to CSA AICM GRC-13 explainability requirements — AI governance objectives must include explainability as a required property; A.5.2-5 objectives and GRC-13 explainability requirements are complementary governance obligations for AI systems.

AI operations (A.7.2-6) map to CSA AICM MDS-01 training pipeline security — AI operational data management must secure the training pipeline; A.7.2-6 operational controls for AI data directly implement MDS-01 training pipeline security requirements.

AI operations (A.7.2-6) map to CSA AICM MDS-02 model artifact scanning — AI operational controls must include scanning of model artefacts for security issues; A.7.2-6 operational data management and MDS-02 model artefact scanning are complementary operational security controls.

AI performance monitoring (A.8.2-5) maps to CSA AICM MDS-08 model integrity checks — AI performance monitoring must include model integrity verification; A.8.2-5 monitoring and MDS-08 integrity checks jointly ensure that AI model outputs have not been compromised.

AI security monitoring (A.8.2-5) maps to CSA AICM MDS-10 model continuous monitoring — continuous monitoring of AI model behaviour required by A.8.2-5 is the ISO 42001 implementation of MDS-10; both controls mandate ongoing surveillance of AI system performance and security.

AI impact assessment (A.9.2-4) maps to CSA AICM MDS-06 adversarial attack analysis — AI impact assessments must include adversarial threat modelling; A.9.2-4 impact assessments and MDS-06 adversarial attack analysis are corollary requirements for evaluating AI system security risks.

AI security controls (A.8.2-5) map to CSA AICM MDS-07 model hardening — AI security measures must include model hardening against adversarial inputs; A.8.2-5 AI security controls and MDS-07 robustness controls are complementary requirements for AI system resilience.

AI governance objectives (A.5.2-5) map to CSA AICM GRC-15 human supervision — human oversight of AI decision-making is both an AI governance objective and a GRC-15 requirement; A.5.2-5 governance objectives must include human-in-the-loop requirements where AI decisions affect individuals.

AI improvement processes (A.10.2-4) map to CSA AICM MDS-11 model failure — AI improvement processes must address model failure scenarios; A.10.2-4 continual improvement must incorporate lessons from model failures and MDS-11 failure response procedures.

AI risk assessment (A.4.2-6) maps to CSA AICM MDS-12 open model risk assessment — AI risk assessments must address risks from use of open-source or publicly available models; A.4.2-6 risk assessment scope should include MDS-12 open model provenance and security evaluation.

AI operations (A.7.2-6) map to CSA AICM AIS-13 AI sandboxing — AI operational environments must use sandboxing and isolation for AI workloads; A.7.2-6 operational controls must address the environment isolation required by AIS-13 to prevent AI workload interference.

AI governance roles (A.3.2-3) map to CSA AICM GRC-14 explainability evaluation — AI governance roles must include responsibility for explainability testing; A.3.2-3 role assignments should allocate GRC-14 explainability evaluation responsibility to the AI governance function.

AI impact assessment (A.9.2-4) maps to CSA AICM MDS-03 model documentation — AI impact assessments require comprehensive model documentation as a prerequisite; A.9.2-4 assessment documentation and MDS-03 model documentation requirements are complementary documentation obligations.
